    AI Overview
    The 25th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, ratified in 1967 following President John F. Kennedy's assassination, clarifies presidential succession and disability
    . It ensures the Vice President becomes President if the President dies, resigns, or is removed, and provides a process for transferring power if the President is incapacitated or unable to discharge their duties. 
    Key Sections of the 25th Amendment: 
    • Section 1 (Succession): Explicitly states that if the President is removed, dies, or resigns, the Vice President becomes President.
    • Section 2 (Vice Presidential Vacancy): Allows the President to nominate a new Vice President if the office becomes vacant, subject to confirmation by a majority vote of both houses of Congress
      .
    • Section 3 (Voluntary Transfer): The President may declare in writing they are unable to perform duties, making the Vice President the Acting President until a written declaration to the contrary is submitted.
    • Section 4 (Involuntary Transfer): Authorizes the Vice President and a majority of the Cabinet (or another body authorized by Congress) to declare the President unable to perform their duties, making the Vice President the Acting President. 
    Invoking Section 4
    Section 4 was designed as a measure of last resort if a President is unable to serve (e.g., due to severe illness) but cannot or will not voluntarily relinquish power. If the President disputes the incapacity, Congress must decide the issue within 48 hours, requiring a two-thirds vote in both houses to keep the Vice President in power. Section 4 has never been formally invoked. 
    Historical Usage 
    • Section 2 (VP Vacancy): Used to appoint Gerald Ford (1973) after Spiro Agnew resigned, and Nelson Rockefeller (1974) after Ford became President.
    • Section 3 (Voluntary): Used by President Reagan in 1985 before surgery, and twice by President George W. Bush in 2002 and 2007 for medical procedures.
